chapter: The Paradise and life in Queens
title: The fire next door, the King Cole Trio cops and what the Paradise taught him
summary: A funny story of firemen, patrolmen who partied at the club and a cop's gun falling out, followed by his reflections on entertaining people.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Till four. Not one minute to four. Four. (laughter) But I loved every minute of it. I remember one time they had a fire next door in the whiskey store. I come to work and the firemen were there and the firemen got them great big boots on and it was just a smoke fire, but they tore that liquor store up and they coiled up and come out there with them bottles of liquor in them big boots and they come next door to our place and, "You got a fire over here?" And they had them hatchets and what not, he says "Where's the money box" or somethin', the cat that was leadin'. I said, "Wait a minute here. There ain't nothin' wrong in here." Gettin' ready to mess up my thing
here...(laughter)...the people who controlled that area...

Yeah...the policeman there was called the King Cole Trio...in a patrol car... that was their beat. So they used to come in there and, shoot, they put on another coat and sit down and enjoy themselves and bring their companion and party like everybody else. So everybody knew 'em, you know, and everything was cool. But one night one of 'em got real happy. He had on a civilian coat and he got on the floor and...he was from Charlestown, South Carolina...and he did that gee-chee dance. He was in time but his gun fell out, (laughter). He was embarrassed, oh my God. But then come to find out the next day, my neighbor, who was two doors from me, he and Scotty used to have a barber shop in Harlem but he and Scotty... was the cop's name...they were long time friends, so they both come to my door and knocked on my door and there was Scotty with his head down and we just fell out. You know, but he remembered what he did last night. (laughter) Oh me, oh my. Then Baby Lawrence used to come in and dance

all night long. My God! Teddy Hill used to come in and dance all night long. But I tried to keep the atmosphere real. The main thing was that we played good music and I was always tryin' to keep the place lively, you know what I mean. Keep people happy. And that job was where I really actually found out about what I'm all about. Nick, you know, what makes me...what motivates me as a musician and as a person and as a person on stage. Now I basically...I love my fellow human being and I guess that was always in me, but it really came to the fore there because I did the best I could to make everyone happy, and all the musicians, to make them comfortable, you know. And then I learned how to M.C., really, and make people laugh and I was, you know, continually growing culturally on my horn, you know, sound-wise, you know. Because I really got into that because I had a job and I was payin' for my house and everything was goin' good, you know. And so I had a chance to relax and get into my horn a little bit more, you know, in the day time. Yeah. I had a tape recorder and I used to bring it over and that thing was heavy, boy, take that thing on the subway and take it on back home. God. (laughter)
